deep.reconstruction:
Context: Euler, Tractatus de numerorum doctrina (E792), Ch. 12, 'On residues from dividing biquadrates by primes'. Throughout, p is an odd prime and R4(p) = {a^4 mod p : p does not divide a}.

§420 (p = 4q-1). The previous page (§§416-417) showed that for such p no two of 1^4, 2^4, ..., (2q-1)^4 are congruent. So |R4| = 2q-1 = (p-1)/2. Every fourth power a^4 = (a^2)^2 is a square, so R4 is contained in R2, the set of quadratic residues. Since |R2| = (p-1)/2 = |R4|, we get R4 = R2. Hence everything said earlier about quadratic residues and non-residues holds verbatim for biquadratic ones when p ≡ 3 mod 4.

§421 (p = 4q+1). Every biquadratic residue α = a^4 satisfies α^q ≡ 1 (mod p).
- Implicit step (mine): α^q = a^{4q} = a^{p-1} ≡ 1 by Fermat.
- R4 is contained in R2, but the converse fails, as shown next.

§422. Every quadratic residue has the form x^2. Suppose every x^2 lay in R4. Then x^{2q} ≡ 1 (mod p) for all x not divisible by p. In particular 1^{2q}-1, 2^{2q}-1, ..., (2q)^{2q}-1 would all be divisible by 4q+1. Euler declares this impossible, so some square is not a biquadratic residue.
- Implicit justification (mine): since (p-x)^{2q} ≡ x^{2q}, the congruence would hold for all 4q residues. But a polynomial of degree 2q has at most 2q roots mod p (Lagrange). Equivalently, Euler's finite-difference argument applies to the 2q+1 consecutive values x = 1, ..., 2q+1, giving (2q)! ≡ 0 mod p, a contradiction.

§423. Let x^2 be a quadratic residue not in R4. Then αx^2, βx^2, ... are also not in R4.
- If αx^2 ≡ b^4, then x^2 ≡ b^4/α would be a fourth-power residue; in modern terms, x^2·R4 is a coset disjoint from R4.
- These products are all quadratic residues, and they are distinct.
- So among the 2q quadratic residues there are at least |R4| that are not biquadratic residues. Hence 2|R4| ≤ 2q, i.e. |R4| ≤ q.
- 'That it is smaller cannot happen' is asserted here and proved on later pages (§§429-435).

§424. Tables of R4 and of the non-residues, arranged in three rows, for p = 5, 13, 17, 29, 37 (q = 1, 3, 4, 7, 9):
- p = 5: R4 = {1}; rows {2}, {4}, {3}.
- p = 13: R4 = {1, 3, 9}; rows {2, 6, 5}, {4, 12, 10}, {8, 11, 7}.
- p = 17: R4 = {1, 4, 13, 16}; rows {3, 12, 5, 14}, {9, 2, 15, 8}, {10, 6, 11, 7}. Here x = 3, because 2^2 = 4 is in R4.
- p = 29: R4 = {1, 16, 23, 24, 20, 7, 25}; rows 2R4, 4R4, 8R4.
- p = 37: R4 = {1, 16, 9, 12, 33, 10, 26, 34, 7}; rows 2R4, 4R4, 8R4.
- In each table row k is x^k·R4 (k = 1, 2, 3), with x = 2 except x = 3 for p = 17.

§425. Induction from the tables: |R4| = q (the upper bound was proved in §423). The non-residues number 3q and split into three classes with distinct properties.

§426. Choose x with x^2 not in R4. Then:
- x is not in R4, else x^2 would be.
- x^3 is not in R4 (implicit, mine: else x^2 = x^6/x^4 would be).
- The three classes are I = x·R4, II = x^2·R4, III = x^3·R4.
- In modern terms: R4 is the index-4 subgroup of (Z/p)^*, the quotient is cyclic of order 4, and x is a generator of the quotient. The next page proves the classes are disjoint and exhaust the non-residues.
errors: §422: the claim that 1^{2q}-1, ..., (2q)^{2q}-1 cannot all be divisible by 4q+1 is stated without proof. With only 2q values, a degree-2q polynomial count does not by itself give a contradiction. One needs the symmetry x -> p-x to obtain 4q roots, or Euler's difference lemma applied to 2q+1 consecutive values. The gap is easily filled but unstated.
§423: 'quod posterius autem fieri nequit' (|R4| < q is impossible) is only asserted here; the proof is deferred to §§429-435 on the next pages.

§424, p = 37: the residue row is printed in the order 1, 16, 9, 12, 33, 10, 26, 34, 7. The three non-residue rows are column-wise 2r, 4r, 8r for the order r = 1, 16, 7, 34, 33, 26, 12, 10, 9, so columns do not align, unlike the tables for 13, 17 and 29. All the sets are nevertheless correct. This is a harmless presentation inconsistency, either Euler's or the editors'.
§426: 'certum est neque x neque x^3 in residuis reperiri posse' is not justified for x^3. It is true, since x^3 = a^4 would make x^2 ≡ x^6·x^{-4} a fourth-power residue.

results.what: For p ≡ 3 mod 4, the biquadratic residues coincide with the quadratic residues.
results.modern_name: For p ≡ 3 (mod 4), the 4th-power map has the same image as squaring, since gcd(4, p-1) = 2.
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (Tractatus, c. 1750); also in Gauss's theory of biquadratic residues (1828)

results.what: A biquadratic residue α mod p = 4q+1 satisfies α^q ≡ 1.
results.modern_name: Euler's criterion for quartic residues: a^{(p-1)/4} ≡ 1 (necessity direction)

results.what: For p = 4q+1, not every quadratic residue is a biquadratic residue, and the number of biquadratic residues is at most q (later shown to be exactly q).
results.modern_name: The 4th powers form an index-4 subgroup of (Z/p)^* (index gcd(4, p-1))
results.usually_credited_to: Euler; Gauss, Disquisitiones (1801) for power residues in general

results.what: Decomposition of the non-residues into three classes x·R4, x^2·R4, x^3·R4, with x^2 a quadratic non-biquadratic residue, illustrated by tables for p = 5, 13, 17, 29, 37.
results.modern_name: Coset decomposition of (Z/p)^* modulo the subgroup of 4th powers (quartic residue characters)
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (Tractatus); systematized by Gauss (Theoria residuorum biquadraticorum, 1828/32)

deep.surprise_reason: This is Euler's Tractatus de numerorum doctrina, published in 1849/1862 and well studied (e.g. in Lemmermeyer's Reciprocity Laws). The page treats elementary structure of biquadratic residues: index of the subgroup, coset classes, and numerical tables. This is known Euler material and routine by modern standards.

checkable.sympy: sorted(set(pow(a,4,29) for a in range(1,29))) == sorted([1,16,23,24,20,7,25])
checkable.asserts: Biquadratic residues mod 29 match Euler's table.
Biquadratic residues mod 37 match Euler's table.
Euler's three non-residue rows for 37 are 2R4, 4R4, 8R4 (column order matching r = 1,16,7,34,33,26,12,10,9).
Euler's non-residue classes for 29 are x^k·R4 with x = 2.
Euler's non-residue classes for 17 are x^k·R4 with x = 3.
Euler's non-residue classes for 13 are x^k·R4 with x = 2.

checkable.sympy: all(len(set(pow(a,4,p) for a in range(1,p)))==(p-1)//4 for p in primerange(5,2000) if p%4==1)
checkable.asserts: For p ≡ 1 mod 4 the number of biquadratic residues is exactly q = (p-1)/4.

checkable.sympy: all(set(pow(a,4,p) for a in range(1,p))==set(pow(a,2,p) for a in range(1,p)) for p in primerange(3,2000) if p%4==3)
checkable.asserts: For p ≡ 3 mod 4 the biquadratic and quadratic residues coincide (§420).

checkable.sympy: all(pow(pow(a,4,p),(p-1)//4,p)==1 for p in primerange(5,500) if p%4==1 for a in range(1,p))
checkable.asserts: §421: α^q ≡ 1 mod 4q+1 for every biquadratic residue α.

transcription_corrections: The transcription agrees with the image; no substantive corrections. OCR 'biquadra!orum' in the image rendering corresponds to 'biquadratorum'. In §422 the image reads '1^{2q}-1, 2^{2q}-1, 3^{2q}-1, 4^{2q}-1, ....(2q)^{2q}-1', consistent with the transcription.
